messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 19
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: African
  relationship_status: In a relationship
  occupation: Detective
  trauma_type: Captivity
  pcl5: 63

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Suppress Thoughts: try hard not think about the trauma, Avoid Night: Going out at night or being outside after dark, Avoid Being Touched: Any form of physical contact with others
  Memory: Cannot Find Words: I know what happened but I am unable to find words to describe it, Auditory Recall: When I have memories of what happened I sometimes hear things in my head that I heard during the frightening event., Emotion Without Image: Sometimes I feel the full emotional intensity of the event without any clear image or memory

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Kwame is a 19-year-old detective who came to treatment after months of trying to manage on his own and finding that his world had narrowed to a set of rules he could no longer keep hidden from the people around him. He is in a relationship, but even in the first sessions he struggled to explain what had happened to him. He would start describing the period when he was held captive during an investigation, stop abruptly, press his palms into his knees, and say he knew exactly what had happened but could not find the words for it. The facts were there in pieces, but when he tried to put them into a narrative, language seemed to fail him.

During the captivity, what stayed with him most vividly were sounds. He had been confined in a dark interior space for stretches of time, unable to predict when someone would enter, and the experience had become encoded less as a coherent story than as fragments of noise and bodily fear. In session, he did not offer dramatic images. Instead he described how certain memories came back with the sound of footsteps approaching, a latch shifting, muffled voices, and the scrape of movement nearby, as if his mind replayed the threatening acoustics before anything else. At other times there was no picture at all. He would suddenly be flooded with the same terror and helplessness he had felt then, his chest tightening and his body bracing, without any clear scene in his mind. What frightened him was not only the memory of being trapped, but the sense that it could seize him without warning and without a story he could tell himself about it.

Those qualities of the memory shaped the way he began living afterward. Because trying to think about the captivity brought back those sounds in his head and, just as often, a wave of raw fear with no image attached, Kwame worked hard to push the whole thing away. He told himself not to go there mentally, cut off conversations if anyone came close to the subject, and kept himself busy rather than risk an unguarded moment. He also began avoiding being outside after dark. Night carried too much of the feeling of that confinement and too much uncertainty about who might be nearby, so he arranged his life to be home before evening whenever he could. Even physical contact became difficult. If his girlfriend reached for his arm unexpectedly or leaned into him, his body reacted before he had time to think, and he pulled away. He understood this looked cold, but to him touch had become bound up with the loss of control he had felt while being held.

These habits have become especially costly in his work. As a detective, he is expected to move through the city at irregular hours, to follow leads that do not wait for daylight, and to stay physically composed in close quarters with colleagues, witnesses, and suspects. Kwame now bargains to avoid nighttime assignments whenever possible, lingering over paperwork or trading tasks to stay inside the station before dark. When he cannot avoid an evening call, he becomes tense and preoccupied, listening for sounds around him in a way that reminds him of the captivity. If a partner claps him on the shoulder or brushes past him in a cramped hallway, he stiffens immediately. He has said little about this at work because he cannot easily explain it; the same difficulty finding words that blocks his account of the trauma also leaves him with no easy way to justify why ordinary parts of the job now feel intolerable.

At home, the pattern has strained his relationship. His girlfriend has tried to be patient, but she has noticed how quickly he shuts down if she asks what happened and how often he seems to disappear into himself. When she reaches for him in bed and he recoils, he feels ashamed, yet he is also certain that if he lets his guard down he will be overwhelmed by the sounds in his head or by that sudden, image-less surge of fear. So he keeps trying not to think, not to talk, not to be touched, not to be out at night, and his life has grown smaller around those efforts.

He sought help after recognizing that the strategy of forcing it all down was not restoring his control. What finally unsettled him was not a single dramatic collapse but the realization that he was organizing his work, his evenings, and his relationship around avoiding anything that might bring the captivity close again. He came in afraid that if he tried to tell the story, the terror would return in full force and he would not be able to stop it. At the same time, he said quietly that he wanted to be able to stand in the dark, hear an ordinary sound, and let the person he loves touch him without feeling as if he were back there.
